name: Tower of London
description: Nearly 1,000 years of history as a royal palace, fortress, and prison. Home to the Crown Jewels and the famous Beefeaters.
tips: Arrive at opening (9am) to see the Crown Jewels before the crowds.

name: British Museum
description: One of the world's greatest museums with a permanent collection of over 8 million works spanning human history. Free entry.
tips: The Rosetta Stone and Egyptian mummies are the star attractions. Consider a guided tour to make the most of your visit.

name: Buckingham Palace & Changing of the Guard
description: The official London residence of the British monarch. Watch the iconic Changing of the Guard ceremony.
tips: Changing of the Guard happens at 11am (check schedule as it varies seasonally). Arrive 45 mins early for a good spot.

name: Westminster Abbey
description: Gothic masterpiece and coronation church of British monarchs since 1066. Final resting place of kings, queens, poets, and scientists.
tips: Visit Poets' Corner to see memorials to Shakespeare, Dickens, and Austen.

name: Natural History Museum
description: A world-class museum housed in a stunning Romanesque building. Famous for its dinosaur exhibits and the spectacular Hintze Hall.
address: Cromwell Rd, South Kensington, London SW7 5BD
tips: Free entry! The building itself is as impressive as the exhibits. Don't miss the Wildlife Photographer of the Year exhibition (ticketed).

name: Tate Modern
description: Britain's national gallery of modern and contemporary art, housed in the former Bankside Power Station on the Thames.
tips: Free permanent collection. The viewing platform on level 10 offers stunning panoramic views of the city.

name: Tower Bridge Exhibition
description: Walk across the high-level glass walkways of London's most iconic bridge and visit the Victorian Engine Rooms.
tips: The glass floor walkway is not for the faint-hearted! Check the bridge lift times on the website.

name: London Eye
description: The iconic observation wheel on the South Bank offering 360-degree views across London from 135 metres high.
address: Riverside Building, County Hall, London SE1 7PB
tips: Book online for cheaper tickets. Sunset rides offer the most spectacular views. Consider the champagne experience for a romantic treat.

name: St Paul's Cathedral
description: Sir Christopher Wren's masterpiece with its world-famous dome. Climb 528 steps to the Golden Gallery for breathtaking views.
tips: Test the Whispering Gallery's acoustics - whisper against the wall and someone on the opposite side can hear you.

name: Victoria and Albert Museum
description: The world's leading museum of art, design and performance. Over 2.3 million objects spanning 5,000 years of creativity.
tips: Free entry. The Fashion Gallery and the Raphael Cartoons are highlights. The museum cafe in the original refreshment rooms is stunning.

name: Hampton Court Palace
description: Henry VIII's magnificent Tudor palace with stunning gardens, the famous maze, and the Great Hall with its hammerbeam roof.
address: Hampton Court Palace, East Molesey KT8 9AU
tips: A full-day excursion. The maze is great fun. Take the train from Waterloo - it's a scenic 35-minute ride.

name: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew
description: UNESCO World Heritage Site with the world's largest collection of living plants. The Victorian glasshouses are architectural marvels.
address: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Richmond TW9 3AE
tips: The Treetop Walkway offers great views. The Palm House is unmissable. Allow at least half a day.

name: Houses of Parliament
description: The iconic Palace of Westminster, home to the UK's democracy. See Big Ben, the Commons Chamber, and Westminster Hall.
tips: Audio tours available on Saturdays and during recess. The view of Big Ben from Westminster Bridge is iconic for photos.

name: National Gallery
description: Home to over 2,300 paintings dating from the 13th century to the early 20th century, including works by Van Gogh, Turner, and da Vinci.
tips: Free entry. Start in the Sainsbury Wing for chronological order. The Sunflowers by Van Gogh is a must-see.

name: Royal Greenwich & the Meridian Line
description: Stand on the Prime Meridian at the Royal Observatory, explore the Maritime Museum, and enjoy views from Greenwich Park.
tips: Take the Thames Clipper from central London for a scenic river trip. The Cutty Sark is worth a visit too.

name: Hyde Park & Kensington Gardens
description: London's largest royal park, perfect for boating on the Serpentine, visiting Speakers' Corner, or simply enjoying a walk.
tips: Rent a pedalo on the Serpentine lake in summer. Visit the Diana Memorial Fountain. Kensington Palace is at the western end.

name: Camden Market
description: London's most famous alternative market with over 1,000 shops and stalls selling everything from vintage fashion to street food.
tips: Best visited on weekends when all stalls are open. The street food section is incredible. Walk along Regent's Canal afterwards.

name: Shakespeare's Globe Theatre
description: A faithful reconstruction of the Elizabethan playhouse where Shakespeare's plays were originally performed.
tips: Standing 'groundling' tickets for performances cost just £5! The guided tour is excellent even without a show.

name: Borough Market
description: London's most renowned food market, operating in some form since 1014. Sample artisanal cheese, fresh oysters, and gourmet street food.
tips: Go hungry! Open Wed-Sat. Friday lunchtimes are lively but less crowded than Saturdays.

name: Warner Bros. Studio Tour - Harry Potter
description: Step onto the actual sets used in the Harry Potter films. See costumes, props, and the incredible Diagon Alley.
tips: Book well in advance - tickets sell out weeks ahead. Allow a full day. The Butterbeer is a must-try!

name: Churchill War Rooms
description: The secret underground headquarters where Churchill and his inner circle directed World War II. Remarkably preserved.
address: Clive Steps, King Charles St, London SW1A 2AQ
tips: The Churchill Museum section is fascinating. Audio guide included in the ticket price.

name: South Bank Cultural Walk
description: A scenic riverside walk from Westminster Bridge to Tower Bridge, passing the London Eye, Tate Modern, Shakespeare's Globe, and Borough Market.
tips: One of London's best free activities. Stop at the second-hand book stalls under Waterloo Bridge. Beautiful at sunset.

name: Notting Hill & Portobello Road
description: Colourful streets, antique shops, and the famous Portobello Road Market. Made iconic by the Hugh Grant film.
tips: Saturday is the main antiques market day. The pastel-coloured houses on Lancaster Road are perfect for photos.

name: Shoreditch Street Art Tour
description: East London's creative heartland, covered in world-class street art by Banksy, Stik, and many other international artists.
tips: Art changes frequently so there's always something new. Brick Lane is nearby for an incredible curry.

name: Sky Garden
description: London's highest public garden at the top of the 'Walkie Talkie' building. Stunning 360-degree views across the city.
tips: Free but must be booked in advance! Sunset slots are the best but fill up fast.

name: West End Theatre Show
description: London's legendary Theatreland with world-class musicals and plays. From long-running hits to exciting new productions.
address: Shaftesbury Avenue / Covent Garden, London WC2
tips: Try the TKTS booth in Leicester Square for same-day discounted tickets. Matinees are usually cheaper.

name: British Library
description: See original manuscripts including the Magna Carta, Shakespeare's First Folio, and handwritten Beatles lyrics.
tips: The Treasures of the British Library gallery is free and absolutely remarkable. Don't miss it.

name: Covent Garden
description: A vibrant piazza with street performers, boutique shops, the Royal Opera House, and an incredible food scene.
tips: Watch the world-class street performers in the piazza. Neal's Yard nearby is one of London's most colourful spots.

name: Abbey Road Studios & Crossing
description: Recreate the iconic Beatles album cover at the famous zebra crossing outside Abbey Road Studios.
tips: Go early morning to avoid traffic and crowds. There's a live webcam so your friends can watch!

name: The View from The Shard
description: Western Europe's tallest building. The viewing platform on floors 68-72 offers views stretching up to 40 miles.
tips: Sunset tickets are more expensive but worth every penny. The open-air platform on floor 72 is exhilarating.

name: Imperial War Museum
description: Powerful and moving museum exploring the causes and consequences of modern conflict from World War I to the present day. The Holocaust Exhibition is profoundly affecting.
tips: Free entry. The atrium with suspended aircraft is spectacular. The Holocaust Exhibition is not recommended for children under 14.

name: Science Museum
description: Interactive science and technology museum with over 15,000 objects on display, from Stephenson's Rocket to the Apollo 10 command module. A paradise for curious minds of all ages.
address: Exhibition Rd, South Kensington, London SW7 2DD
tips: Free entry. The IMAX cinema and flight simulator are ticketed extras. Wonderlab is brilliant for children but gets busy at weekends.

name: Museum of London (London Museum)
description: Tells the story of London and its people from prehistoric times to the present. Relocated to a stunning new home in the former Smithfield General Market building.
tips: Free entry. The recreated Victorian street scenes are a highlight. Combined well with a visit to nearby Smithfield Market.

name: Horniman Museum & Gardens
description: A wonderfully eclectic museum with natural history, musical instruments, and anthropology collections set in beautiful hillside gardens. The overstuffed walrus is an icon.
address: 100 London Rd, Forest Hill, London SE23 3PQ
tips: Free entry to the museum and gardens. The butterfly house is a small ticketed extra. Stunning views across London from the gardens.

name: Design Museum
description: Dedicated to contemporary design in every form, from architecture and fashion to graphics and product design. Housed in a beautifully restored 1960s modernist building.
tips: The permanent collection is free. Temporary exhibitions are ticketed but consistently excellent. The museum shop is a great place for unique gifts.

name: Sir John Soane's Museum
description: The wonderfully eccentric former home of the architect Sir John Soane, crammed with antiquities, paintings, and architectural models. A hidden gem in Lincoln's Inn Fields.
tips: Free entry. The Picture Room with its fold-out walls revealing hidden Hogarth paintings is unforgettable. Candlelit evening openings on the first Tuesday of each month.

name: Wellcome Collection
description: A fascinating free museum exploring the connections between medicine, life, and art. Thought-provoking exhibitions that challenge how we think about health and the human body.
tips: Free entry. The Reading Room is a beautiful space to relax. Temporary exhibitions are always inventive and surprising.

name: Trafalgar Square
description: London's most famous public square, dominated by Nelson's Column and flanked by the National Gallery. A gathering point for celebrations, protests, and everyday London life.
tips: Check the Fourth Plinth for the latest contemporary art commission. The fountains are beautifully lit at night.

name: Piccadilly Circus
description: The bright lights of London's most iconic junction, home to the famous illuminated advertising screens and the Eros statue. The beating heart of the West End.
tips: Best experienced after dark when the lights are most impressive. A great starting point for exploring Soho, Chinatown, or the West End theatres.

name: The Monument to the Great Fire of London
description: Climb 311 steps up this 62-metre Doric column designed by Sir Christopher Wren to commemorate the Great Fire of 1666. Rewarding panoramic views from the top.
tips: One of London's best-value viewpoints. Buy a joint ticket with Tower Bridge Exhibition to save money. You get a certificate for climbing to the top.

name: Leadenhall Market
description: A stunning Victorian covered market in the heart of the City of London, dating back to the 14th century. Its ornate painted roof and cobbled floors featured as Diagon Alley in the Harry Potter films.
tips: Visit on a weekday lunchtime when the market is buzzing with City workers. The optician's shop at 42 Bull's Head Passage was used as the entrance to the Leaky Cauldron.

name: The Royal Exchange
description: A grand neoclassical building founded in 1571 by Sir Thomas Gresham as a centre of commerce. Now home to luxury boutiques and a beautiful central courtyard bar and restaurant.
tips: The Fortnum & Mason bar in the central courtyard is a lovely spot for afternoon tea. Look up at the stunning ceiling and murals.

name: Regent's Park & Queen Mary's Gardens
description: An elegant royal park with formal gardens, a boating lake, and an open-air theatre in summer. Queen Mary's Gardens contain over 12,000 roses in spectacular displays.
tips: The Open Air Theatre runs from May to September with excellent Shakespeare and musical productions. The rose gardens peak in June.

name: Richmond Park
description: London's largest royal park and a National Nature Reserve, home to over 600 free-roaming red and fallow deer. A glorious escape from the city with ancient oak trees and sweeping meadows.
tips: Early morning is best for deer photography. The view from King Henry's Mound to St Paul's Cathedral (12 miles away) is protected by law. Cycling is a great way to explore.

name: Primrose Hill
description: A small but perfectly formed park offering one of the most celebrated panoramic views of the London skyline. The surrounding village has a charming literary and celebrity heritage.
tips: Sunset and sunrise are magical here. Combine with a walk along Regent's Canal from Camden. The high street has lovely independent cafes and bookshops.

name: Battersea Park
description: A beautiful Victorian park on the south bank of the Thames with a boating lake, a children's zoo, and stunning riverside walks. The Peace Pagoda is a serene highlight.
tips: The riverside promenade has great views of Chelsea. Visit the children's zoo for a budget-friendly family outing. The sub-tropical gardens are a hidden treat.

name: Columbia Road Flower Market
description: A riot of colour and fragrance every Sunday morning on this narrow East End street. Independent shops, galleries, and cafes line the road, opening only on market day.
tips: Sundays only, 8am-3pm. Arrive early for the best selection or late for bargains as traders reduce prices. The surrounding shops sell vintage homewares and artisan goods.

name: Broadway Market
description: A trendy East London Saturday market with artisan food stalls, vintage clothes, and a buzzing local atmosphere. Flanked by the Regent's Canal and London Fields park.
tips: Saturdays only. The street food is outstanding - try the toasties from The Cheese Truck. Walk along the canal to Victoria Park afterwards.

name: Portobello Road Antiques Market
description: The world's largest antiques market with over 1,000 dealers selling everything from Georgian silverware to vintage fashion. The southern end near Notting Hill Gate has the finest antiques.
tips: Saturday is the main antiques day. The market stretches nearly a mile and changes character as you walk north - antiques give way to food, fashion, and bric-a-brac.

name: Thames Clippers River Bus
description: London's river bus service is the most scenic commute in the world. Hop on at piers across the city for sweeping views of Parliament, the Tower, Canary Wharf, and Greenwich.
address: Various piers across London (Westminster, Embankment, Bankside, Tower, Greenwich)
tips: Use an Oyster card or contactless for cheaper fares. The route from Westminster to Greenwich is the most scenic. Sit on the open-air rear deck in good weather.

name: Emirates Air Line Cable Car
description: A cable car crossing high above the Thames between Greenwich Peninsula and the Royal Docks, offering dramatic views of Canary Wharf, the O2, and the Thames Barrier.
tips: Pay with Oyster or contactless for the cheapest fare. The experience cabin (extra cost) offers a longer ride and a glass of bubbly. Best at sunset.

name: Little Venice Canal Walk
description: A picturesque stretch of canal where Regent's Canal meets the Grand Union Canal, lined with colourful narrowboats and weeping willows. Walk the towpath all the way to Camden Lock.
tips: Take a narrowboat trip from Little Venice to Camden through Regent's Park and London Zoo. The waterside Puppet Theatre Barge is a unique treat for families.

name: Hampstead Heath Walk
description: An ancient and wild heathland covering 790 acres of rolling hills, ancient woodland, and swimming ponds. Parliament Hill offers arguably the finest panoramic view of London.
tips: Swim in the bathing ponds in summer (separate ponds for men, women, and mixed). Kenwood House at the northern end has a free art collection and a lovely cafe.

name: Highgate Cemetery
description: A magnificent Victorian cemetery with dramatic Gothic architecture, overgrown catacombs, and the graves of Karl Marx, George Eliot, and Douglas Adams. Atmospheric and hauntingly beautiful.
tips: The atmospheric West Cemetery can only be visited on a guided tour (book ahead). The East Cemetery (where Marx is buried) can be visited independently.

name: Dennis Severs' House
description: A unique and immersive time-capsule experience in a Georgian townhouse in Spitalfields. Each room is set as if the Huguenot silk-weaver inhabitants have just stepped out, complete with sounds and smells.
tips: The Monday evening candlelit 'Silent Night' visits are the most atmospheric - book well in advance. No talking or photography allowed inside; just absorb it.

name: Crossness Pumping Station
description: A breathtaking example of Victorian industrial architecture, described as the cathedral of sewage. The ornamental ironwork by Joseph Bazalgette is some of the finest in the world.
address: The Old Works, Bazalgette Way, London SE2 9AQ
tips: Open days are limited (usually monthly) so check the website and book ahead. The restored Beam Engine House with its colourful Romanesque ironwork is jaw-dropping.

name: Leighton House Museum
description: The former studio-home of the Victorian painter Frederic, Lord Leighton. The Arab Hall, with its shimmering gold mosaic dome and collection of Islamic tiles, is one of London's most beautiful rooms.
tips: A genuine hidden gem - rarely crowded. The Arab Hall alone is worth the visit. Combine with nearby Holland Park for a lovely half-day.

name: The Postal Museum & Mail Rail
description: Explore the history of the Royal Mail and ride the Mail Rail, a miniature train through the tunnels of London's secret underground postal railway that operated from 1927 to 2003.
tips: The Mail Rail ride is the star attraction - a genuine underground railway beneath the streets of London. Book the combined ticket. Children love it.

name: Museum of the Home (Geffrye Museum)
description: Explores the home and how we have lived in it from 1600 to the present day through a series of beautifully recreated period rooms. Set in gorgeous 18th-century almshouses with lovely gardens.
tips: Free entry. The period gardens behind the almshouses are a delight, especially in spring and summer. The museum cafe is excellent.

name: Brighton Day Trip
description: London's favourite seaside escape, just an hour by train. The eclectic Lanes shopping area, the flamboyant Royal Pavilion, Brighton Pier, and a thriving food scene make it a perfect day out.
address: Brighton, East Sussex (trains from London Victoria/St Pancras)
tips: Direct trains from Victoria or St Pancras take about 1 hour. The Royal Pavilion is unmissable. Walk along the seafront from the pier to Hove for fish and chips.

name: Windsor Castle Day Trip
description: The oldest and largest occupied castle in the world, and a favourite weekend residence of the King. See the State Apartments, St George's Chapel, and the Changing of the Guard.
address: Windsor Castle, Windsor SL4 1NJ (trains from London Paddington/Waterloo)
tips: Direct trains from Paddington (25 min) or Waterloo (55 min). St George's Chapel is where Harry and Meghan married. The town of Windsor is charming for lunch.

name: Stonehenge Coach Tour from London
description: Visit the world's most famous prehistoric monument, a UNESCO World Heritage Site dating back over 4,500 years. Most tours combine Stonehenge with Bath or Windsor for a full-day excursion.
address: Stonehenge, Salisbury SP4 7DE (coach tours depart from central London)
tips: Book a combined Stonehenge and Bath tour for the best value. The visitor centre exhibition is excellent. Inner circle access tours are available at dawn and dusk for an extra fee.

name: Tate Britain
description: The national gallery of British art from 1500 to the present, housing the world's greatest collection of works by J.M.W. Turner. The annual Turner Prize exhibition is a highlight.
tips: Free entry. Take the free Tate Boat between Tate Britain and Tate Modern for a scenic Thames trip. The Pre-Raphaelite rooms are magnificent.

name: Soho Food & Nightlife Exploration
description: London's most vibrant neighbourhood for eating and drinking, packed with independent restaurants, historic pubs, cocktail bars, and late-night haunts. From Chinatown dumplings to Berwick Street espresso.
tips: Bar Italia for late-night espresso, Ronnie Scott's for jazz, and Chinatown for dim sum. Berwick Street Market is great for a daytime visit.

name: ZSL London Zoo
description: The world's oldest scientific zoo, opened in 1828, set within Regent's Park. Home to over 750 species including Sumatran tigers, western lowland gorillas, and Humboldt penguins.
address: Outer Circle, Regent's Park, London NW1 4RY
tips: Book online for significantly cheaper tickets. The Land of the Lions and Gorilla Kingdom are highlights. Feeding times add extra excitement.

name: Brick Lane
description: The heart of London's Bangladeshi community and a hub of street art, vintage shopping, and some of the best curry houses in the city. Sunday is market day with food stalls stretching the length of the street.
tips: Visit on a Sunday for the full market experience. The Beigel Bake at No. 159 serves legendary salt beef beigels 24/7. Don't be swayed by the curry house touts - ask locals for recommendations.

name: Kensington Palace
description: A working royal palace and former home of Queen Victoria, Princess Diana, and now the Prince and Princess of Wales. The King's and Queen's State Apartments reveal centuries of royal life.
tips: The Sunken Garden outside the palace is beautiful and free to visit. Combined well with a walk through Kensington Gardens and Hyde Park.

name: Wembley Stadium Tour
description: Go behind the scenes at England's national football stadium. Walk down the players' tunnel, see the Royal Box, sit in the manager's dugout, and lift a replica FA Cup.
tips: Tours run daily but check for event-day closures. The walk up Olympic Way (Wembley Way) towards the arch is iconic.

name: Cricket at The Oval
description: Watch world-class cricket at one of the sport's most historic grounds, home to Surrey County Cricket Club since 1845. International matches and domestic games throughout the summer.
address: The Kia Oval, Kennington, London SE11 5SS
tips: County matches are affordable and atmospheric. International Test match tickets sell out fast. You can bring your own food and drink (no glass).

name: The Wallace Collection
description: An outstanding collection of fine and decorative arts housed in a grand 18th-century townhouse. Masterpieces by Titian, Rembrandt, Velazquez, and Frans Hals alongside one of the finest armouries in the world.
address: Hertford House, Manchester Square, London W1U 3BN
tips: Free entry. The Great Gallery with its Old Master paintings is superb. The courtyard restaurant under the glass roof is a beautiful spot for lunch.

name: Courtauld Gallery
description: One of the finest small art collections in the world, housed in the grand Somerset House on the Strand. Impressionist and Post-Impressionist masterpieces by Manet, Renoir, Cezanne, and Van Gogh.
tips: Manet's Bar at the Folies-Bergere is the star piece. Free entry for under 18s. Somerset House itself has a lovely courtyard fountain in summer and ice rink in winter.

name: Dulwich Picture Gallery
description: England's oldest purpose-built public art gallery, designed by Sir John Soane in 1817. A gem of a collection featuring Rembrandt, Poussin, Gainsborough, and Canaletto in intimate, light-filled rooms.
tips: Free on Fridays. The beautiful gardens and surrounding Dulwich Village with its Georgian houses make for a lovely half-day trip. Combine with Dulwich Park.

name: National Army Museum
description: The story of the British Army from the English Civil War to modern-day peacekeeping. Interactive galleries with uniforms, weapons, art, and personal stories of soldiers across the centuries.
tips: Free entry. The Soldier gallery with personal stories is moving. The kids' play zone is excellent for young families. Near the Royal Hospital Chelsea.

name: Hayward Gallery
description: One of the UK's most important venues for major contemporary art exhibitions. The brutalist architecture of the South Bank Centre is striking, and the rooftop sculpture terrace offers Thames views.
address: Southbank Centre, Belvedere Rd, London SE1 8XX
tips: Exhibitions change regularly and are always thought-provoking. Check what's on before visiting. The Southbank Centre food market outside is great for a pre-visit lunch.

name: Whitechapel Gallery
description: A pioneering gallery championing contemporary art since 1901, giving early UK exposure to Picasso, Pollock, and Rothko. Continues to show cutting-edge work in the heart of East London.
tips: Free entry to most exhibitions. The gallery cafe and bookshop are both excellent. Easy to combine with a walk around Spitalfields and Brick Lane.

name: Serpentine Galleries
description: Two gallery spaces in the heart of Kensington Gardens showing major exhibitions of contemporary art and architecture. The annual summer Pavilion by a world-famous architect is a highlight.
tips: Free entry. Visit between June and October to see the Serpentine Pavilion. The walk between the two galleries through Kensington Gardens is lovely.

name: National Portrait Gallery
description: Home to the world's most extensive collection of portraits, from Tudor monarchs to contemporary figures. Recently reopened after a major refurbishment with a stunning new entrance and galleries.
tips: Free entry. Start at the top floor with the Tudors and work down through the centuries. The rooftop restaurant has stunning views over Trafalgar Square.

name: National Maritime Museum
description: The world's largest maritime museum, exploring Britain's relationship with the sea through art, maps, manuscripts, and ship models. Set in a magnificent neoclassical building in Greenwich.
tips: Free entry. Nelson's bullet-holed coat from Trafalgar is a highlight. The Great Map in the children's gallery is brilliant for families.

name: Fan Museum
description: The world's only museum dedicated to the art and craft of fans, housed in two restored Georgian townhouses in Greenwich. Over 5,000 fans dating from the 11th century to the present day.
tips: A delightfully quirky small museum. The fan-making workshops are a unique experience. The Japanese-style garden and orangery serve afternoon tea on Tuesdays and Sundays.

name: Foundling Museum
description: Tells the powerful story of the Foundling Hospital, Britain's first children's charity established in 1739. Features an outstanding collection of art donated by Hogarth, Handel manuscripts, and moving personal tokens left by mothers.
tips: The tokens left by mothers forced to give up their babies are incredibly moving. Handel was a major benefactor and his connection is well told. The park outside is lovely.

name: Brunel Museum
description: Celebrates the engineering genius of Marc and Isambard Kingdom Brunel at the site of the Thames Tunnel, the first tunnel ever built under a navigable river. Descend into the atmospheric underground Grand Entrance Hall.
tips: The underground shaft is atmospheric and occasionally hosts concerts and events. A short walk from Rotherhithe station. Great combined with a Thames-side walk.

name: Cartoon Museum
description: Dedicated to the art of cartoons, caricature, comics, and animation from the 18th century to the present. From Hogarth satires and Punch cartoons to contemporary graphic novels and manga.
tips: A cheerful small museum with regularly changing exhibitions. The shop has excellent graphic novels and cartoon prints. Near the British Museum for a combined visit.

name: Petrie Museum of Egyptian & Sudanese Archaeology
description: One of the world's greatest collections of Egyptian and Sudanese archaeology, tucked away in University College London. Over 80,000 objects including the oldest known garment and early examples of metallurgy.
tips: Free entry. A real insider's museum - torches are provided to peer into darkened cases. Much quieter than the British Museum with equally fascinating objects.

name: Bank of England Museum
description: Explore the history of the Bank of England from its founding in 1694 to its role today. Handle a real gold bar, see historic banknotes, and learn about the financial systems that shaped the modern world.
tips: Free entry. Lifting the gold bar is a surprisingly fun experience. Weekday only opening, so plan accordingly. A nice addition to a City of London walk.

name: London Transport Museum
description: The story of London's transport network from horse-drawn omnibuses to the Tube. Vintage buses, original Underground carriages, and iconic Johnston typeface and Beck Tube map design.
tips: Your ticket is valid for a year of unlimited returns. Children under 18 go free. The vintage poster collection is outstanding and the shop sells great reproductions.

name: Holland Park & Kyoto Garden
description: An elegant park in the heart of Kensington featuring the enchanting Kyoto Garden, a Japanese-style garden with a waterfall, koi carp, and free-roaming peacocks. The ruins of Holland House add a romantic backdrop.
tips: The Kyoto Garden is one of London's most serene spots. Peacocks roam freely. Opera Holland Park performs in the ruins of the house each summer.

name: Victoria Park
description: East London's beloved green space, known as the People's Park. Two lakes, an excellent playground, a pagoda, and a vibrant Sunday market make it a favourite for local families.
tips: The Pavilion Cafe by the lake is a wonderful brunch spot. Visit on Sunday mornings to combine with Broadway Market. The park hosts major festivals in summer.

name: St James's Park
description: The oldest of London's Royal Parks, offering iconic views of Buckingham Palace across the lake. Home to pelicans (fed daily at 2:30pm) and a rich variety of waterfowl in the heart of Westminster.
tips: The pelicans have been residents since 1664. The view from the Blue Bridge across the lake with Buckingham Palace behind is one of London's finest vistas.

name: Green Park
description: A peaceful triangular park connecting Buckingham Palace to Piccadilly, notable for its mature trees and absence of formal flowerbeds. In spring, the park is carpeted with daffodils.
tips: The most tranquil of the central Royal Parks. Beautiful for deckchair lounging in summer. A convenient cut-through between Buckingham Palace and the West End.

name: Crystal Palace Park
description: A grand Victorian pleasure park famous for its extraordinary life-size dinosaur sculptures from 1854, the world's first attempt to model extinct animals. The terraces mark where Paxton's Crystal Palace once stood.
tips: The dinosaur sculptures are wonderfully charming - scientifically inaccurate but historically fascinating. The maze and children's playground are great for families.

name: Alexandra Palace & Park
description: Known as the People's Palace, this grand Victorian entertainment venue sits atop a hill in North London with 196 acres of parkland. Home to the world's first regular public TV broadcasts by the BBC in 1936.
tips: The panoramic views of the London skyline from the terrace are among the best in the city. The ice rink, boating lake, and farmers' market are all popular.

name: Maltby Street Market
description: A hidden gem beneath the railway arches of Bermondsey, this Saturday market is where London's foodies go to escape the Borough Market crowds. Outstanding artisan producers and street food.
tips: Saturdays 10am-5pm, Sundays 11am-4pm. Much less crowded than Borough Market with equally good food. The Waffle On and St John Bakery stalls are legendary.

name: Old Spitalfields Market
description: A beautifully restored Victorian market hall in the heart of East London. Fashion, vintage, art, and food stalls operate daily, with the best selection on Thursdays and weekends.
tips: Thursday is antiques day, Friday is fashion, and the weekend has the widest variety. The surrounding streets have great independent shops and restaurants.

name: Greenwich Market
description: A covered craft and food market in the heart of Greenwich's UNESCO World Heritage Site. Artisan crafts, antiques, and international street food in a charming setting near the Cutty Sark.
tips: Open daily but best on weekends. The craft stalls sell unique handmade gifts. Combine with visits to the Cutty Sark, Royal Observatory, and Greenwich Park.

name: Berwick Street Market
description: One of London's oldest street markets, running through the heart of Soho since the 1840s. A vibrant mix of fresh produce, street food, vinyl records, and vintage finds.
tips: Weekday lunchtimes are the best time for street food. The surrounding independent record shops make this a pilgrimage for music lovers. Featured on the Oasis album cover.

name: Alfies Antique Market
description: London's largest indoor antique market, spread over four floors of a former department store. Over 75 dealers selling vintage fashion, mid-century furniture, Art Deco jewellery, and collectibles.
tips: Tuesday to Saturday only. The rooftop cafe is a lovely spot. Church Street itself has more antique shops stretching towards Edgware Road.

name: Bermondsey Antique Market
description: A long-established Friday morning antique market where dealers buy from each other under torchlight before dawn. Silverware, jewellery, paintings, and curios fill Bermondsey Square from early morning.
tips: Friday mornings only, from 6am. The earliest buyers get the best finds. A unique London experience - arrive at dawn for the full atmosphere.

name: Banqueting House
description: The last surviving part of the Palace of Whitehall, designed by Inigo Jones in 1622. The magnificent ceiling paintings by Rubens are among the finest in Europe. Charles I walked through this hall to his execution.
tips: The Rubens ceiling paintings are breathtaking - there are mirrors on tables so you can study them without craning your neck. Check for occasional closures for government events.

name: Eltham Palace
description: A fascinating blend of medieval royal palace and 1930s Art Deco mansion. The Great Hall dates from the 1470s while the Courtauld family's interiors are a masterpiece of Jazz Age glamour, including a heated cage for their pet lemur.
tips: The Art Deco interiors are stunning and the moated medieval gardens are beautiful. A real off-the-beaten-track gem. English Heritage members enter free.

name: Apsley House (Wellington Museum)
description: The grand London residence of the Duke of Wellington, known as 'No. 1 London' for its prestigious address at Hyde Park Corner. Houses Wellington's art collection including works by Velazquez and a colossal nude statue of Napoleon.
address: 149 Piccadilly, Hyde Park Corner, London W1J 7NT
tips: The Waterloo Gallery where the annual Waterloo Banquet was held is magnificent. The giant Canova statue of Napoleon that Wellington kept as a trophy is wonderfully ironic.

name: Jewel Tower
description: One of only two surviving buildings from the original medieval Palace of Westminster, built in 1365 to house Edward III's treasures. A small but fascinating survival in the shadow of Parliament.
tips: A peaceful medieval escape steps from Parliament. The exhibition about Parliament past and present is informative. English Heritage members enter free.

name: Two Temple Place
description: An astonishing late-Victorian neo-Gothic mansion built for William Waldorf Astor in the 1890s. Lavish interiors with stained glass, carved wood, and bronze fittings. Hosts free exhibitions from regional museum collections.
tips: Free entry but only open during exhibitions (usually January to April). The building itself is the star - every surface is decorated. Check the website for exhibition dates.

name: Kenwood House
description: A stunning neoclassical villa on the northern edge of Hampstead Heath, housing the Iveagh Bequest of Old Master paintings including a Vermeer and a Rembrandt self-portrait. The Robert Adam library is sublime.
tips: Free entry. The lakeside concerts in summer are magical. Combine with a walk across Hampstead Heath. The Brew House cafe does excellent cakes.

name: Southwark Cathedral
description: The oldest Gothic church in London, with parts dating to the 12th century. Shakespeare's brother Edmund is buried here, and John Harvard, founder of Harvard University, was baptised in the building.
tips: Free entry (donations welcome). A peaceful contrast to nearby Borough Market. The retrochoir is the oldest Gothic structure in London. Lunchtime concerts are a treat.

name: Temple Church
description: A 12th-century church built by the Knights Templar with a striking circular nave modelled on the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. Made famous by The Da Vinci Code, it contains remarkable stone effigies of medieval knights.
tips: The round nave is atmospheric and the knight effigies are remarkable. Limited opening hours so check before visiting. The surrounding Temple Inn gardens are a peaceful escape.

name: St Bartholomew the Great
description: London's oldest surviving parish church, founded in 1123, with a magnificent Norman interior. Featured in Four Weddings and a Funeral, Shakespeare in Love, and The Other Boleyn Girl.
tips: The atmospheric Norman arch entrance through the 13th-century gatehouse is spectacular. Free to enter for worship. The surrounding Cloth Fair area is charming.

name: Westminster Cathedral
description: The mother church of Roman Catholics in England and Wales, built in a striking neo-Byzantine style with distinctive banded brickwork. The bell tower offers panoramic views over Westminster.
tips: Free entry to the cathedral. The tower lift costs about £8 and offers great views. Often confused with Westminster Abbey - they are two different buildings! The marble interior is magnificent.

name: St Martin-in-the-Fields
description: An iconic 18th-century church on Trafalgar Square, famous for its concerts by candlelight. The free lunchtime concerts and excellent Cafe in the Crypt make it a must-visit.
tips: Free lunchtime concerts on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Fridays. The evening candlelit concerts are magical. The Cafe in the Crypt is a unique and atmospheric place to eat.

name: St Dunstan in the East
description: A hauntingly beautiful ruined church destroyed in the Blitz and transformed into a secret garden. Gothic arches draped in climbing plants create one of London's most photogenic hidden gems.
tips: Open during daylight hours. Visit in the morning for the best light and fewer crowds. The surviving Wren steeple is beautiful. A perfect Instagram spot.

name: Battersea Power Station
description: The iconic Grade II-listed power station, famous from the Pink Floyd album cover, reborn as a spectacular shopping, dining, and entertainment destination. Ride the glass lift up the northwest chimney for stunning views.
tips: The Lift 109 chimney experience costs about £16 for panoramic views. The food hall and riverside restaurants are excellent. Connected by the Northern Line extension.

name: Coal Drops Yard
description: A stunning shopping and dining destination created from two Victorian coal drops buildings where coal from the north was once unloaded from trains. The dramatic 'kissing roofs' architecture by Heatherwick Studio is breathtaking.
tips: The architecture where the two roofs curve to meet is incredible. Great independent shops and restaurants. The Granary Square fountains next door are fun for children.

name: King's Cross Granary Square
description: A vibrant public square at the heart of the King's Cross regeneration, featuring 1,080 individually controlled fountains, canal-side dining, and the striking Central Saint Martins art school building.
tips: The choreographed fountains are a delight for children in summer. The Regent's Canal runs alongside with pleasant towpath walks. Excellent restaurants and the House of Illustration nearby.

name: The O2
description: London's premier entertainment arena on the Greenwich Peninsula. Beyond concerts and events, climb Up at The O2 for an exhilarating walk across the roof of the dome with panoramic views.
tips: The Up at The O2 climbing experience is thrilling - sunset and twilight climbs are the most popular. Book well in advance. Arrive early for events as the venue is huge.

name: Printworks London
description: A massive former printing facility in Canada Water transformed into one of London's most dramatic event and nightlife venues. Its vast industrial spaces host immersive events, exhibitions, and world-class DJ sets.
tips: Check the programme online - events sell out fast. The sheer scale of the venue is awe-inspiring. Daytime events have a very different vibe to the nighttime parties.

name: Peckham Levels
description: A disused multi-storey car park transformed into a thriving creative hub with independent food vendors, bars, studios, and event spaces. A symbol of South London's creative energy.
tips: The rooftop bar has great views. The street food vendors are varied and affordable. A good starting point for exploring Peckham's vibrant food and art scene.

name: Parliament Hill Viewpoint
description: The most famous viewpoint on Hampstead Heath, offering a sweeping panorama of the London skyline from the Shard to Canary Wharf. A protected view corridor ensures the vista remains unobstructed.
address: Parliament Hill, Hampstead Heath, London NW5 1QR
tips: Sunrise and sunset are the most rewarding times. Kite flying is popular on windy days. The athletics track and lido are at the base of the hill.

name: Royal Observatory Greenwich Viewpoint
description: Stand on the Prime Meridian line and enjoy panoramic views over the Queen's House, the Old Royal Naval College, and the Thames stretching to Canary Wharf and beyond.
tips: The viewpoint in Greenwich Park is free - you only pay to enter the Observatory itself. The time ball drops at 1pm daily. The view at sunset is spectacular.

name: Tower Bridge Glass Walkway
description: Walk across the high-level glass floor walkways 42 metres above the Thames for a thrilling bird's-eye view of London's river traffic and city landmarks.
tips: Included in the Tower Bridge Exhibition ticket. The glass floor panels are vertiginous but thrilling. Try to time your visit with a bridge lift for the ultimate view.

name: SEA LIFE London Aquarium
description: One of Europe's largest aquariums, located in the former County Hall on the South Bank. Walk through an underwater tunnel surrounded by sharks, rays, and a colony of Gentoo penguins.
address: County Hall, Westminster Bridge Rd, London SE1 7PB
tips: Book online for up to 40% off. The shark walk and penguin feeding times are highlights. Combined tickets with the London Eye offer good savings.

name: Madame Tussauds
description: The world's most famous wax museum, featuring lifelike figures of celebrities, world leaders, sports stars, and cultural icons. The Spirit of London ride and Star Wars experience add extra thrills.
tips: Book online well in advance for the cheapest tickets. Off-peak time slots are significantly cheaper. The Marvel 4D experience is a fun addition.

name: London Dungeon
description: A theatrical walk-through experience bringing London's gruesome history to life with live actors, special effects, and rides. Jack the Ripper, the Great Plague, and Sweeney Todd all feature.
address: County Hall, Westminster Bridge Rd, London SE1 7PB
tips: Not suitable for very young children. Book online for cheaper tickets. The actors are brilliantly entertaining. Combined tickets with nearby attractions offer savings.

name: Shrek's Adventure! London
description: An immersive walk-through adventure set in the world of Shrek, featuring a magical 4D bus ride and encounters with characters from the films. Great fun for families with younger children.
address: County Hall, Westminster Bridge Rd, London SE1 7PB
tips: Best for children aged 3-10. Book online for cheaper tickets. Combined with other Merlin attractions on the South Bank for a full family day.

name: KidZania London
description: A child-sized city where kids aged 4-14 can try over 60 real-life jobs, from firefighter and pilot to surgeon and journalist. They earn KidZos currency and learn about the working world through play.
address: Westfield London, Ariel Way, London W12 7GF
tips: Book in advance and arrive early as children get absorbed for hours. Best for ages 4-14. Adults enter for a reduced fee. Allow at least 3-4 hours.

name: Diana Memorial Playground
description: A magical pirate ship-themed playground in Kensington Gardens, inspired by Peter Pan. The huge wooden ship, teepees, and sensory trail make it one of London's best playgrounds for young children.
tips: Free entry. Only children accompanied by an adult can enter. Can get busy on weekends and school holidays - arrive early. The Peter Pan statue nearby is worth seeking out.

name: Harrods
description: The world's most famous department store, a London institution since 1849. Seven floors of luxury goods, from the spectacular Food Halls to high fashion, homewares, and the Egyptian-themed escalators.
tips: The Food Halls are spectacular even if you're not buying. Free to enter and browse. A dress code applies (no ripped jeans or activewear). Visit during the week to avoid weekend crowds.

name: Liberty London
description: A department store like no other, housed in a magnificent Tudor Revival building constructed from the timbers of two Royal Navy ships. Famous for its floral print fabrics, Liberty is a temple to craftsmanship and design.
tips: The building itself is beautiful - look up at the Tudor timber frame. The haberdashery department is legendary for craft lovers. The Christmas shop is magical.

name: Selfridges
description: An iconic Oxford Street department store founded by Harry Gordon Selfridge in 1909. Known for its extraordinary window displays, innovative retail concepts, and the famous Food Hall.
tips: The window displays are always creative - worth seeing from the outside alone. The rooftop has hosted a cinema, bowling alley, and forest. The Food Hall rivals Harrods.

name: Fortnum & Mason
description: The Queen's grocer since 1707, this elegant Piccadilly store is famous for its teas, hampers, and the iconic clock where mechanical figures of Mr Fortnum and Mr Mason emerge on the hour.
tips: Afternoon tea in the Diamond Jubilee Tea Salon is a quintessentially London experience (book ahead). The ground floor food hall is wonderful for gifts and treats.

name: Carnaby Street
description: The legendary Swinging Sixties street, now a pedestrianised shopping district with independent boutiques, restaurants, and Kingly Court food hall. The area retains its colourful, rebellious spirit.
tips: Kingly Court has three floors of independent restaurants and bars. The side streets like Newburgh Street have the best independent shops. Seasonal decorations are always spectacular.

name: King's Road Chelsea
description: The birthplace of punk and the Swinging Sixties fashion revolution, now an upscale shopping street mixing high-end boutiques with heritage brands. The Saatchi Gallery and Duke of York Square add cultural weight.
tips: The Saatchi Gallery at Duke of York Square is free. The Saturday farmers' market at Duke of York Square is excellent. Walk the full length from Sloane Square to World's End.

name: Seven Dials
description: A charming meeting point of seven streets in Covent Garden, radiating from a central sundial pillar. Independent shops, beauty brands, theatres, and excellent restaurants fill the cobbled lanes.
address: Seven Dials, Covent Garden, London WC2H 9HD
tips: The sundial column in the centre actually has six sundials (not seven!). Great independent shops and a strong beauty and wellness scene. The Cambridge Theatre (Matilda) is right here.

name: God's Own Junkyard
description: A dazzling warehouse of vintage and salvaged neon signs crammed floor to ceiling, in a Walthamstow industrial estate. The life's work of neon artist Chris Bracey, it feels like stepping into a neon-lit fever dream.
address: Unit 12, Ravenswood Industrial Estate, Shernhall St, London E17 9HQ
tips: Free entry (donations welcome). Open weekends only. One of London's most photogenic spaces. The Rolling Scones cafe inside is excellent. A bit out of the way but absolutely worth the trip.

name: Leake Street Graffiti Tunnel
description: A legal graffiti tunnel beneath Waterloo Station where artists continuously paint and repaint the walls. Also known as Banksy Tunnel after the artist held his Cans Festival here in 2008.
tips: Free and always open. The art changes constantly so every visit is different. You might see artists at work. A great photo opportunity near the South Bank.

name: Brixton Village & Market Row
description: A vibrant covered market in the heart of Brixton with a global food scene, independent boutiques, and a strong community spirit. Two connected market arcades offer everything from Caribbean food to Vietnamese pho.
tips: The restaurant scene is excellent and affordable. Try Franco Manca (which started here) or Chishuru for contemporary West African food. First Fridays has a party atmosphere.

name: The Hill Garden & Pergola
description: A secret Edwardian raised walkway and pergola draped in wisteria and climbing plants, hidden on the edge of Hampstead Heath. One of London's most romantic and least-known treasures.
address: Inverforth Close, North End Way, London NW3 7EX
tips: Free entry. The wisteria blooms spectacularly in May. One of London's best-kept secrets. Access is through a small gate off North End Way - easy to miss.

name: Postman's Park
description: A small tranquil park near St Paul's, home to the Memorial to Heroic Self-Sacrifice - a wall of ceramic plaques commemorating ordinary people who died saving others. Featured in the film Closer.
tips: The memorial plaques are deeply moving - each tells a story of extraordinary bravery by ordinary people. A peaceful lunch spot for City workers. Free and always open.

name: Phoenix Garden
description: A hidden community garden tucked behind Charing Cross Road in the heart of the West End. Created on a WWII bomb site, this wildlife-friendly oasis is a secret green retreat from the bustle of Theatreland.
tips: Free entry. A genuine hidden gem - most Londoners don't know it exists. Perfect for a quiet moment between West End shows. Frogs, newts, and hedgehogs live here.

name: Crossrail Place Roof Garden
description: A tropical and temperate garden housed under a spectacular latticed timber roof at Canary Wharf. Plants from the Americas, Asia, and Europe grow in this striking modern space above the Elizabeth line station.
tips: Free entry. A surprisingly peaceful escape above the Canary Wharf bustle. The timber roof structure is architecturally stunning. Occasional free performances and events.

name: The Cenotaph
description: Britain's primary war memorial, standing in the centre of Whitehall. Designed by Edwin Lutyens and unveiled in 1920, it is the focus of the national Remembrance Sunday ceremony each November.
tips: Free to visit at any time. The simple design is deliberately non-denominational. Best appreciated as part of a walk along Whitehall from Trafalgar Square to Parliament Square.

name: Mudchute Park & Farm
description: The largest city farm in Europe, set on 32 acres on the Isle of Dogs with stunning views of Canary Wharf. Over 100 animals including llamas, pigs, goats, and horses. A surreal countryside-in-the-city experience.
address: Pier St, Isle of Dogs, London E14 3HP
tips: Free entry. The juxtaposition of farm animals and Canary Wharf skyscrapers is surreal and wonderful. The Mudchute Kitchen cafe is excellent. Great for families.

name: The Line Sculpture Walk
description: London's first dedicated contemporary art walk, following the Meridian line from the O2 through the Royal Docks to the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park. Free outdoor sculptures by major artists including Damien Hirst and Antony Gormley.
address: The Line, Greenwich Peninsula to Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park
tips: Free and always accessible. Download the free app for a guided walk. The route follows waterways and passes through regenerated areas. Some sculptures are only visible at low tide.

name: Charles Dickens Museum
description: The only surviving London home of Charles Dickens, where he lived from 1837 to 1839 and wrote Oliver Twist and Nicholas Nickleby. Beautifully restored rooms filled with manuscripts, personal items, and first editions.
tips: The desk where Dickens wrote Oliver Twist is a highlight. Special Christmas events bring Victorian celebrations to life. A must for literature lovers.

name: Keats House
description: The Hampstead home where John Keats lived from 1818 to 1820, where he fell in love with Fanny Brawne and wrote some of his finest poems including Ode to a Nightingale. A place of genuine literary pilgrimage.
tips: The garden where Keats heard the nightingale is peaceful. Poetry readings and events are held regularly. Combine with a walk to Hampstead Heath and the Spaniards Inn pub.

name: Sherlock Holmes Museum
description: A lovingly recreated Victorian townhouse at 221B Baker Street, exactly as described in Arthur Conan Doyle's stories. Rooms are dressed as if Holmes and Watson have just stepped out.
tips: Join the queue early as capacity is limited and waits can be long. The gift shop is excellent. Pose with the deerstalker and pipe in Holmes's sitting room.

name: Daunt Books Marylebone
description: One of the most beautiful bookshops in the world, housed in an Edwardian building with long oak galleries, skylights, and William Morris-style details. Books are arranged by country, making it perfect for travel planning.
tips: The back room with its galleried shelves and stained-glass skylight is stunning. The travel section arranged by country is inspired. Regular author events.

name: Foyles
description: A legendary independent bookshop on Charing Cross Road since 1903, now in a stunning modern five-storey flagship building. Over 200,000 books across four miles of shelving, with a rooftop cafe and gallery.
tips: The top-floor cafe has views over the rooftops of Soho. Major author events and book launches are held regularly. The children's floor is excellent.

name: Alexandra Palace Viewpoint
description: One of London's finest panoramic viewpoints from the south-facing terrace of Alexandra Palace. On a clear day, you can see the entire London skyline from the Shard to Wembley Arch.
tips: Free and always accessible. Bring a picnic on a clear day. The pub inside the Palace has outdoor seating with the same view. Sunset is particularly stunning.

name: National Theatre
description: One of the world's great theatre companies, staging an extraordinary range of new plays and classics in three auditoria on the South Bank. The brutalist building by Denys Lasdun is a landmark.
tips: Friday Rush tickets at £15 are released each Friday for the following week's performances. Backstage tours are fascinating. The free exhibitions in the foyer are worth a visit.

name: Royal Albert Hall
description: One of the world's most iconic concert venues, hosting the annual BBC Proms since 1941. This magnificent Victorian amphitheatre seats nearly 5,300 and has hosted everyone from Wagner to Adele.
tips: Proms standing tickets (Prommers) cost just £8. Guided tours run daily when no events are on. The terrace has lovely views over Hyde Park.

name: Ronnie Scott's Jazz Club
description: London's most famous jazz club, open since 1959 in the heart of Soho. An intimate venue that has hosted Miles Davis, Ella Fitzgerald, and every major jazz artist. World-class live music seven nights a week.
tips: Late-night shows after 11pm are cheaper. Book ahead for headline acts. The atmosphere is intimate and the sound quality is superb. Dinner and show packages available.

name: Hampstead Village
description: A charming hilltop village that has attracted artists and writers for centuries. Georgian streets, independent bookshops, cosy pubs, and leafy lanes make it feel like a country village transported to London.
tips: Walk through Flask Walk and Well Walk for the most picturesque lanes. The Holly Bush and The Flask are excellent historic pubs. Continue to the Heath for the full experience.

name: Royal Opera House
description: The home of The Royal Opera and The Royal Ballet in a stunning theatre in Covent Garden. Backstage tours, free lunchtime concerts in the foyer, and world-class performances make it accessible to all.
tips: Same-day tickets and standing spots can be very affordable. The Linbury Theatre has smaller, often cheaper productions. Free lunchtime recitals in the Paul Hamlyn Hall are a delight.

name: Barbican Centre
description: Europe's largest multi-arts centre, housed in a spectacular brutalist complex in the City of London. Concert hall, theatres, cinemas, galleries, a tropical conservatory, and a stunning lakeside setting.
tips: The Conservatory is free but must be booked (open Sundays). The brutalist architecture is extraordinary. The Curve gallery is free. Getting lost in the estate is part of the experience.

name: Somerset House
description: A magnificent neoclassical building on the Strand with a grand courtyard featuring dancing fountains in summer and an ice rink in winter. Free exhibitions, the Courtauld Gallery, and riverside terrace.
tips: The courtyard fountains (55 jets) are a children's delight in summer. Free exhibitions rotate regularly. The river terrace cafe has lovely Thames views.

name: Saatchi Gallery
description: A leading contemporary art gallery in the Duke of York's HQ building in Chelsea, showing major exhibitions of emerging and established artists. The elegant Georgian military building provides a striking contrast to the art within.
address: Duke of York's HQ, King's Rd, London SW3 4RY
tips: Free entry to most exhibitions. Always showing something provocative and conversation-starting. The Duke of York Square Saturday market outside is excellent.

name: Cutty Sark
description: The world's last surviving tea clipper, beautifully restored and raised on a glass platform so you can walk beneath her gleaming copper hull. A testament to the age of sail and global trade.
address: King William Walk, Greenwich, London SE10 9HT
tips: Walking beneath the hull is magical. Combined tickets with the Royal Observatory offer savings. The collection of figureheads in the lower hold is fascinating.

name: Old Royal Naval College - Painted Hall
description: The Painted Hall at the Old Royal Naval College is known as Britain's Sistine Chapel. James Thornhill's baroque ceiling and wall paintings covering 40,000 square feet took 19 years to complete.
address: King William Walk, Greenwich, London SE10 9NN
tips: The ceiling painting is breathtaking. Lie on the provided bean bags to study the ceiling without neck strain. The grounds and Chapel are free to visit.

name: Chelsea Physic Garden
description: London's oldest botanic garden, founded in 1673 by the Worshipful Society of Apothecaries. A tranquil walled garden growing medicinal, edible, and useful plants from around the world in the heart of Chelsea.
tips: The Garden of Medicinal Plants is fascinating. The cafe is lovely for afternoon tea. Open April to October with limited winter opening. A peaceful Chelsea gem.

name: Whitechapel Bell Foundry Site & Neighbourhood
description: The former site of Britain's oldest manufacturing company (1570-2017), which cast Big Ben and the Liberty Bell. The surrounding Whitechapel neighbourhood is rich in East End history and immigrant heritage.
tips: The foundry building still stands and plans for a heritage centre are underway. The surrounding streets are steeped in East End history. Combine with the Whitechapel Gallery.

name: Neal's Yard
description: A hidden courtyard of brightly painted buildings tucked away in Covent Garden, home to health food shops, holistic therapies, and the famous Neal's Yard Dairy cheese shop. One of London's most colourful corners.
tips: The cheese shop (Neal's Yard Dairy) on Shorts Gardens is a must for food lovers. The courtyard is extremely photogenic. Often missed by visitors who don't know the narrow entrance.

name: Lord's Cricket Ground Tour
description: The Home of Cricket since 1814. The behind-the-scenes tour takes you through the Long Room, the dressing rooms, the famous slope, and the outstanding MCC Museum housing the original Ashes urn.
address: St John's Wood Rd, London NW8 8QN
tips: The Long Room is magnificent. Tours run daily unless there's a match. The Ashes urn in the museum is surprisingly small. Combine with nearby Abbey Road.

name: Chelsea FC Stadium Tour
description: Go behind the scenes at Stamford Bridge, home to Chelsea Football Club since 1905. Visit the dressing rooms, walk through the tunnel, and see the trophy room with its collection of silverware.
address: Stamford Bridge, Fulham Rd, London SW6 1HS
tips: Tours don't run on match days or the day before European matches. The museum has memorabilia spanning over a century. Book online for guaranteed entry.

name: Wimbledon Lawn Tennis Museum & Tour
description: Go behind the scenes at the world's most prestigious tennis tournament. See Centre Court, No.1 Court, and the museum with its collection of tennis memorabilia spanning 200 years.
tips: Tours run year-round except during The Championships (late June-July). The 200-degree cinema experience is immersive. Championship tickets are allocated by ballot - enter the previous year.

name: Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park
description: The legacy of the 2012 Olympics, now a vibrant parkland with world-class sporting venues, the ArcelorMittal Orbit sculpture, playgrounds, and gardens along the River Lea.
address: Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, London E20 2ST
tips: The park is free to explore. The ArcelorMittal Orbit (about £17) has the world's longest tunnel slide. The London Aquatics Centre designed by Zaha Hadid is stunning.

name: London Wetland Centre
description: A remarkable urban nature reserve in Barnes, created from four disused Victorian reservoirs. Over 180 species of bird have been recorded on this 105-acre site, just four miles from central London.
tips: Early morning is best for birdwatching. Otters, bitterns, and kingfishers are all resident. The adventure playground is excellent for children. Binoculars available to borrow.

name: Greenwich Foot Tunnel
description: A remarkable Edwardian pedestrian tunnel running beneath the Thames, connecting Greenwich to the Isle of Dogs. The 370-metre tiled tunnel with its domed glass entrances has been carrying foot traffic since 1902.
tips: Free and open 24 hours. The circular glass-domed entrance buildings are handsome. Walking under the Thames is a unique London experience. Lifts available if you prefer not to use the spiral stairs.

name: Spitalfields Heritage Walk
description: A walk through one of London's most historically layered neighbourhoods, from the magnificent Nicholas Hawksmoor church to Georgian silk merchants' houses, Jack the Ripper's Whitechapel, and today's thriving markets.
tips: Start at Christ Church Spitalfields (Hawksmoor's masterpiece). Fournier Street has the finest Georgian houses. Combine with Dennis Severs' House and Brick Lane for a full day.

name: Regent's Canal Walk
description: A scenic towpath walk along the Regent's Canal from Little Venice through London Zoo, Regent's Park, Camden Lock, King's Cross, and Islington. See a different side of London from the waterway.
address: Regent's Canal, London (Little Venice to Limehouse)
tips: The full walk from Little Venice to Limehouse is about 8.5 miles. The stretch from Little Venice to Camden Market is the most popular section. Look out for herons and kingfishers.

name: Woolwich Foot Tunnel & Dockyard
description: Walk beneath the Thames through this Edwardian pedestrian tunnel and explore the historic Royal Arsenal and Woolwich Dockyard regeneration area with riverside walks, museums, and artillery heritage.
tips: The Firepower Royal Artillery Museum and the restored Royal Arsenal buildings are fascinating. The riverside walk is pleasant. Less touristy than central London.

name: Chinatown London
description: A vibrant neighbourhood around Gerrard Street packed with Chinese and East Asian restaurants, bakeries, and supermarkets. The ornamental gates, lanterns, and Chinese New Year celebrations make it a sensory feast.
tips: Chinese New Year celebrations in late January or February are spectacular. Try dim sum for a classic experience. The bakeries sell excellent pastries and buns at bargain prices.

name: London Mithraeum (Bloomberg SPACE)
description: The reconstructed Roman Temple of Mithras, discovered in 1954 and now beneath the Bloomberg European headquarters. A free immersive experience reveals the 1,800-year-old temple with light and sound.
tips: Free but must be booked online. The underground experience revealing the temple is atmospheric and well done. Roman artefacts on display upstairs. A remarkable survival beneath modern London.

name: London Museum of Water & Steam
description: Housed in a magnificent Victorian pumping station at Kew Bridge, this museum tells the story of London's water supply through the world's largest collection of Cornish beam engines. The engines are steamed on weekends.
tips: Visit on weekends when the engines are steamed - seeing them in operation is mesmerising. The outdoor water play area is fantastic for children in summer.

name: Inns of Court
description: The four ancient Inns of Court - Lincoln's Inn, Gray's Inn, Inner Temple, and Middle Temple - form a network of atmospheric courtyards, gardens, and halls dating back centuries. A world of legal tradition hidden in plain sight.
address: The Inns of Court, London WC2A / EC4Y
tips: The grounds are free to walk through on weekdays. Lincoln's Inn Fields is the largest public square in London. The Temple Gardens by the Thames are peaceful. Middle Temple Hall has one of the finest Elizabethan interiors in London.

name: Chiswick House & Gardens
description: A stunning Palladian villa built by Lord Burlington in 1729, surrounded by 65 acres of beautiful gardens that inspired the English Landscape Garden movement. The conservatory houses world-class camellias.
tips: The gardens are free and beautiful year-round. The camellia collection blooms in February-March. English Heritage members enter the house free. A serene escape from central London.

name: Platform 9 3/4 - King's Cross
description: The famous Harry Potter trolley disappearing into the wall between platforms 9 and 10 at King's Cross Station. A free photo opportunity with a trolley and choice of House scarves, plus an official Harry Potter shop.
tips: Free photo taken by staff, or use your own camera. Queues can be long at weekends - visit early on weekday mornings. The Harry Potter shop next door sells every Hogwarts item imaginable.

name: Hunterian Museum
description: A fascinating and occasionally gruesome medical museum at the Royal College of Surgeons, displaying surgical instruments, anatomical specimens, and the skeleton of the 7ft 7in Irish Giant. Reopened after major refurbishment.
tips: Free entry. Not for the squeamish! The surgical history collection is fascinating. Combine with Sir John Soane's Museum on the same square.

name: Islington Upper Street & Chapel Market
description: A vibrant North London high street packed with gastropubs, independent restaurants, theatres, and boutiques. The vintage shops, Almeida Theatre, and the traditional Chapel Market give it authentic character.
tips: The Almeida Theatre has an excellent reputation for new work. Camden Passage (not Camden Market) has charming antique shops and a Wednesday market. Excellent pub scene.

name: Kensington High Street & Design Quarter
description: A grand shopping street anchored by the Design Museum and leading to the hidden gem of Holland Park. The surrounding streets house independent boutiques, antique shops, and some of London's finest residential architecture.
tips: The Kensington Church Street antiques dealers are world-renowned. The Design Museum is at the western end. Walk through Holland Park for a complete afternoon.

name: Osterley Park & House
description: One of the last surviving great country estates in London, with a magnificent Robert Adam-designed interior and 357 acres of parkland. The grand portico and neoclassical rooms are exceptionally well preserved.
tips: National Trust property. The Adam interiors are exceptional, especially the Etruscan Dressing Room. The parkland is free to walk in. A genuine countryside feeling despite being in suburban London.

name: Camley Street Natural Park
description: A small but precious urban nature reserve on the Regent's Canal, just steps from the bustle of King's Cross. Wildflower meadows, woodland, ponds, and over 300 species of plant thrive in this two-acre wildlife haven.
tips: Free entry. A remarkable pocket of nature beside the canal. Frogs, dragonflies, and kingfishers are regularly spotted. The new visitor centre has information about urban wildlife.

name: Bermondsey Street Walk
description: A charming South London street that has transformed from industrial to artsy, lined with independent galleries, restaurants, cocktail bars, and the White Cube gallery. The old tannery buildings give it character.
tips: The White Cube gallery is free. Pizarro and Casse-Croute are excellent restaurants. Walk south to the Fashion and Textile Museum. Best combined with Maltby Street Market on Saturdays.

name: Brixton Windmill
description: A working Georgian windmill in the heart of Brixton, one of only two surviving windmills in inner London. Built in 1816, it has been lovingly restored and grinds flour for local bakeries.
address: Windmill Gardens, Blenheim Gardens, London SW2 5EU
tips: Free guided tours on weekends (check schedule). The sight of a windmill in the middle of Brixton is wonderfully surreal. The flour is sold at local markets.

name: Deptford Market Yard
description: An authentic South London street market with a mix of traditional traders and trendy food stalls. One of London's most culturally diverse and unpretentious markets, with Caribbean food, vintage clothes, and local life.
tips: Saturday is the main market day. The Deptford Market Yard has newer artisan food stalls alongside the traditional street market. Very local and authentic.

name: Dulwich Village
description: A charming South London village with Georgian and Victorian buildings, independent shops, excellent pubs, and Dulwich Park. The Dulwich Picture Gallery, Dulwich College, and the toll gate add to its timeless character.
tips: The last toll gate in London still operates on College Road. Dulwich Park is lovely for a walk. The Crown & Greyhound pub has a great beer garden. Combine with the Picture Gallery.

name: Fashion & Textile Museum
description: Founded by designer Zandra Rhodes, this vivid orange and pink museum in Bermondsey hosts excellent exhibitions on fashion, textiles, and design from the 20th and 21st centuries.
tips: The building itself is eye-catching. Exhibitions rotate and are consistently well-curated. The shop sells unique textiles and accessories. Combine with a Bermondsey Street walk.

name: Garden Museum
description: A charming museum dedicated to the art, history, and design of gardens, housed in the medieval church of St Mary-at-Lambeth next to Lambeth Palace. The knot garden and plant collections are delightful.
tips: The medieval tower offers views over Lambeth Palace and the Thames. Captain Bligh of the Bounty is buried in the churchyard. The cafe is excellent.

name: Shard Restaurants & Bars
description: Dining at altitude in Western Europe's tallest building, with restaurants and bars from floors 31 to 52 offering spectacular views without the observation deck ticket price. Aqua Shard, Hutong, and Oblix lead the way.
tips: Aqua Shard serves afternoon tea with views - cheaper than the observation deck and you get food. Book a window table well in advance. The bar at Oblix West has no minimum spend.

name: Clerkenwell & Exmouth Market
description: A historic neighbourhood where medieval monasteries, Georgian townhouses, and modern design studios sit side by side. Exmouth Market's lunch stalls, Spa Fields, and the Museum of the Order of St John add depth.
tips: Exmouth Market food stalls are excellent at lunchtime. Moro and Morito restaurants are legendary. The Priory Church of St John is free to visit. A neighbourhood for foodies and architecture lovers.

name: Peckham Rye Park & Common
description: A beautiful South London park with a Japanese garden, ornamental lake, and wild common. William Blake reportedly saw angels in an oak tree here as a child. The surrounding area buzzes with creative energy.
tips: The Japanese garden and ornamental lake are lovely. The Common has a wilder feel. Combine with a visit to Peckham Levels and the area's excellent restaurants.

name: Thames Barrier & Information Centre
description: The world's second-largest movable flood barrier, protecting London from tidal surges. The Information Centre explains how this remarkable feat of engineering works and why London needs it.
tips: The barrier is most impressive during test closures (check schedule). The riverside walk has good views. The Information Centre has a working model. Combine with the nearby Greenwich Peninsula.

name: Marylebone High Street
description: One of London's most charming high streets, lined with independent boutiques, delis, a weekend farmers' market, and some of the city's best restaurants. A sophisticated village atmosphere in central London.
tips: The Sunday farmers' market in the Conran carpark is excellent. Daunt Books is a must-visit. La Fromagerie cheese shop is outstanding. The Marylebone Lane backstreets have hidden gems.

name: Old Operating Theatre Museum & Herb Garret
description: The oldest surviving surgical operating theatre in Europe, hidden in the attic of a Baroque church near London Bridge. Dating from 1822, it pre-dates anaesthetics and antiseptics - operations were brutal, fast, and public.
tips: The spiral staircase access is narrow and steep. Weekend demonstrations of Victorian surgery bring history vividly to life. A unique and slightly gruesome London experience.

name: London Fields Lido
description: A heated 50-metre outdoor swimming pool in the heart of Hackney, open year-round. One of London's last remaining lidos, it attracts hardy swimmers in winter and sun-seekers in summer.
tips: Heated to 25 degrees year-round. Early morning swims are the most peaceful. London Fields park alongside is great for a picnic. Gets very busy on sunny summer weekends.

name: Fulham Palace
description: The former country home of the Bishops of London for over 1,200 years, set in 13 acres of botanical gardens beside the Thames in Fulham. A hidden gem with Tudor, Georgian, and Victorian elements.
tips: Free entry to the palace and grounds. The botanical garden is delightful. The Drawing Room cafe is lovely. Thames-side walks lead to Putney Bridge.

name: Hackney City Farm
description: A friendly community farm in the heart of Hackney with pigs, goats, sheep, donkeys, and poultry. The farm cafe serves excellent Italian food using ingredients from the farm's own garden.
tips: Free entry. The Italian cafe is surprisingly excellent. The pottery studio offers workshops. Small but perfectly formed - great for young families. Near Broadway Market.

name: Canary Wharf Public Art Trail
description: One of Europe's largest collections of public art, with over 90 sculptures, installations, and artworks by leading artists scattered throughout the Canary Wharf estate. A free open-air gallery in an unlikely setting.
tips: Free and always accessible. Download the art trail map from the Canary Wharf website. Works by Henry Moore, Lynn Chadwick, and Allen Jones among others. The underground stations also feature commissioned art.

name: Walthamstow Wetlands
description: Europe's largest urban wetland nature reserve, spread across 211 hectares of Victorian reservoirs in North East London. Home to herons, cormorants, and rare bitterns, with stunning views of the city skyline.
tips: Free entry. Early mornings are best for birdwatching. The Engine House visitor centre is in a beautifully converted Victorian building. Bring binoculars for the bird hides.

name: South Kensington Museums Quarter Walk
description: A walk through Exhibition Road connecting three world-class free museums - Natural History, Science, and V&A - plus the Royal Albert Hall and Imperial College. Prince Albert's vision of a cultural quarter brought to life.
tips: All three major museums are free. The Albert Memorial in Kensington Gardens is stunning. Exhibition Road itself was redesigned as a shared space. You could easily spend an entire day here.

name: Hackney Wick Creative Quarter
description: A former industrial area beside the Olympic Park transformed into one of Europe's densest creative communities. Canal-side warehouses house artist studios, craft breweries, galleries, and the vibrant Grow cafe-bar.
tips: The canal towpath walk from Hackney Wick to Victoria Park is lovely. Crate Brewery does excellent pizza by the canal. Open studio weekends (usually in May) let you explore artists' workspaces.

name: Stratford & Olympic Legacy Walk
description: A walk through the transformed East London landscape around Stratford, from the grand Stratford International station through the Olympic Park, past the London Stadium, Aquatics Centre, and the ArcelorMittal Orbit to the vibrant East Village.
tips: The walk is free and well-signposted. Westfield Stratford City is nearby for shopping and food. The Velodrome and Copper Box Arena host regular public events. The parklands are beautiful in spring.
